claim: Degree distributions in protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are believed to follow a power law (PL).
source: Degree distributions in protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are believed to follow a power law (PL).
evidence: This is a statement about the current belief in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Technical and study biases affect the experimental procedures for detecting PPIs.
source: However, technical and study biases affect the experimental procedures for detecting PPIs.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: Cancer-associated proteins have received disproportional attention.
source: For instance, cancer-associated proteins have received disproportional attention.
evidence: This is presented as an example of study bias.

claim: Bait proteins in large-scale experiments tend to have many false-positive interaction partners.
source: Moreover, bait proteins in large-scale experiments tend to have many false-positive interaction partners.
evidence: This is stated as a known issue with experimental methods.

claim: Study bias and technical bias suffice to produce the observed PL distribution in PPI networks.
source: Our findings are supported by mathematical models and extensive simulations, and indicate that study bias and technical bias suffice to produce the observed PL distribution.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by mathematical models and simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: It is problematic to derive hypotheses about the topology of the true biological interactome from the PL distributions in observed PPI networks.
source: It is, hence, problematic to derive hypotheses about the topology of the true biological interactome from the PL distributions in observed PPI networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: PL-distributed networks have a small world property with relatively high resilience against random perturbations.
source: Another feature of PL-distributed networks is their small world property, where a small network diameter leads to relatively high resilience against random perturbations (Cohen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a cited property of PL-distributed networks.

claim: The PL property seems to describe common features of diverse networks such as food webs, metabolic networks, the internet, and PPI networks.
source: This commonality in the topology of real-world networks is considered a universal law, as it seems to describe common features of such diverse networks such as food webs, metabolic networks, the internet, and (PPI) networks (Jeong et al., 2001; Barabási and Oltvai, 2004; Yook et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a cited claim about the universality of power laws in networks.

claim: Protein families involved in general biological processes such as protein folding, gene regulation, or post-translational modifications are very promiscuous and bind to a large number of other proteins.
source: Protein families that are involved in general biological processes such as protein folding, gene regulation, or post-translational modifications are very promiscuous and bind to a large number of other proteins, whereas the majority of proteins show few interactions (Nobeli et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a cited biological explanation for the PL property.

claim: In the evolution of networks, new vertices attach preferentially to sites that are already well connected.
source: Moreover, it is crucial for the emergence of the PL property that, in the evolution of networks, 'new vertices attach preferentially to sites that are already well connected' (Barabasi and Albert, 1999).
evidence: This is a cited mechanism for the emergence of power laws.

claim: In the evolution of PPI networks, preferential attachment can be explained via gene duplication and subsequent mutation.
source: It has been suggested that, in the evolution of PPI networks, such preferential attachment can be explained via gene duplication and subsequent mutation (Pastor-Satorras et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a cited hypothesis about the biological mechanism.

claim: The assumption that PPI networks show a PL distribution has been codified in textbooks and training material.
source: Today, the assumption that PPI networks show a PL distribution has been codified in textbooks (Barabási and Pósfai, 2016) and training material (Millán, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to textbooks and training materials.

claim: Some studies use PL fittings as quality criteria for their measured networks.
source: Some studies use PL fittings as quality criteria for their measured networks Stelzl et al., 2005; others use topological protein properties ex- or implicitly for predicting disease genes (Xu and Li, 2006; Janyasupab et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that use this approach.

claim: WGCNA and CEMiTool use the assumption that biological networks are PL-distributed to inform the automated choice of hyper-parameters.
source: Further examples are the co-expression module inference tools WGCNA (Zhang and Horvath, 2005; Langfelder and Horvath, 2008) and CEMiTool (Russo et al., 2018). In these tools, the assumption that biological networks are PL-distributed directly informs the automated choice of hyper-parameters used to prune or transform the co-expression matrices, i.e., the hyper-parameters are chosen such that the resulting degree distributions yield good PL fits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the tools and description of their methodology.

claim: WGCNA has more than 17,000 citations according to Google Scholar as of February 2024.
source: Since WGCNA is extremely widely used (more than 17,000 citations according to Google Scholar as of February 2024), the PL assumption has hence potentially shaped the results reported in thousands of studies.
evidence: This is a verifiable fact from Google Scholar.

claim: PL properties of networks across disciplines often lack statistical support or mechanistic backing.
source: Even though it was reported that PL properties of networks across disciplines often lack statistical support or mechanistic backing (Stumpf and Porter, 2012), the assumption that PPI networks are PL-distributed has become mainstream in the network biology field.
evidence: This is a cited critical perspective on power laws in networks.

claim: Various studies challenge the correctness of the claim that empirical PPI networks are scale-free or PL-distributed.
source: Broadly, these studies can be categorized in two groups. Firstly, various studies exist that challenge the correctness of the claim that empirical PPI networks are scale-free or PL-distributed (Pržulj et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2005; Khanin and Wit, 2006; Lima-Mendez and van Helden, 2009; Przulj et al., 2010; Broido and Clauset, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to critical studies.

claim: Some studies use goodness-of-fit tests to show that PL distributions do not provide a good fit of the empirical degree distributions in some empirical PPI networks.
source: In some of these studies, goodness-of-fit tests are used to show that, in some empirical PPI networks, PL distributions actually do not provide a good fit of the empirical degree distributions (Tanaka et al., 2005; Khanin and Wit, 2006; Lima-Mendez and van Helden, 2009; Broido and Clauset, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using this methodology.

claim: Some studies argue that simulated non-PL networks are often more similar to empirical PPI networks than simulated PL networks.
source: In others, networks are simulated using random network generation models that do and do not yield PL-distributed networks, and it is then argued that the simulated non-PL networks are often more similar to empirical PPI networks than the simulated PL networks (Pržulj et al., 2004; Przulj et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using this approach.

claim: Some studies challenge that PL distribution in empirical PPI networks is sufficient evidence to conclude that the same holds for the ground truth interactome.
source: Second, there are studies which concede (at least for the sake of the argument) that empirical PPI networks are PL-distributed, but challenge that this is sufficient evidence to conclude that the same holds for the ground truth interactome (Stumpf et al., 2005; Han et al., 2005; Deeds et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to critical studies.

claim: The aggregated human PPI network consists of 41,862 studies and a total of 471,693 unique interactions among 17,865 proteins.
source: To confirm this, we aggregated a large human PPI network consisting of 41,862 studies and a total of 471,693 unique interactions among 17,865 proteins.
evidence: This is data from the study's analysis.

claim: When considering networks of size 200 or larger, there were approximately 3.5 times as many non-PL-distributed networks as compared to PL-distributed networks.
source: We observed that when considering networks of size 200 or larger, there were approximately 3.5 times as many non-PL-distributed networks as compared to PL-distributed networks (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 84% of the 739 single-study networks with at most 20 PPIs are classified as PL-distributed.
source: E. g., 84% of the 739 single-study networks with at most 20 PPIs (a network size which we consider unlikely to lead to reasonable degree distribution fits) are classified as PL-distributed.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: More than 50% of PL aggregated networks were obtained after the aggregation of non-PL studies.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, we obtained more than 50% of PL aggregated networks after the aggregation of non-PL studies.
evidence: This is a result from the aggregation experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The more studies merged, the greater the fraction of PL studies (from 53 to 83%).
source: In particular, the more studies we merged, the greater the fraction of PL studies (from 53 to 83%), demonstrating that the PL property can emerge from the aggregation of non-PL networks.
evidence: This is a result from the aggregation experiment.

claim: In 9 out of 27 cases, PL degree distributions were turned into non-PL degree distributions by applying bait usage correction.
source: We observed that in 9 out of the 27 cases, we turned PL degree distributions into non-PL degree distributions by applying this correction.
evidence: This is a result from the correction analysis.

claim: Prey hubs are most strongly enriched for 'protein folding' and 'chaperone-mediated protein folding'.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the prey hubs are most strongly enriched for 'protein folding' and 'chaperone-mediated protein folding' (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The majority of human proteins require assistance in folding by chaperones.
source: Since the majority of human proteins require assistance in folding by chaperones (Fink, 1999), they might indeed be true hub proteins.
evidence: This is a cited biological fact.

claim: Chaperones compose 10% of the cellular proteome mass in humans.
source: As chaperones compose 10% of the cellular proteome mass in humans (Finka and Goloubinoff, 2013), we were concerned that the enrichment of chaperones among the prey hubs could be an artifact of a detection bias of AP-MS toward highly abundant proteins.
evidence: This is a cited biological fact.

claim: Uncorrected hubs are associated with many different types of diseases, in particular with cancer.
source: The disease gene enrichment analysis confirms the previous observation that uncorrected hubs are associated with many different types of diseases (Figure 6—source data 1), in particular with cancer (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from disease enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Prey hubs exhibit an enrichment of diseases related to the nervous system.
source: Prey hubs exhibit an enrichment of diseases related to the nervous system (though much weaker as compared to the enrichment of cancer among the uncorrected hubs).
evidence: This is a result from disease enrichment analysis.

claim: Normalized and Y2H hubs do not show any significant enrichment in diseases.
source: In contrast, normalized and Y2H hubs do not show any significant enrichment in diseases, challenging the idea that disease genes per se have a higher connectivity in PPI networks.
evidence: This is a result from disease enrichment analysis.

claim: Protein misfolding is a hallmark of many nervous system diseases.
source: This is likely because protein misfolding is a hallmark of many nervous system diseases (Tittelmeier et al., 2020; Nucifora et al., 2019) and indeed chaperones play a role in the prevention of misfolding.
evidence: This is a cited biological fact.

claim: The observed PL behavior of empirical PPI networks obtained via aggregation of AP-MS studies tells us very little about the topology of the ground truth interactome.
source: The results summarized above hence indicate that the observed PL behavior of empirical PPI networks obtained via aggregation of AP-MS studies tells us very little about the topology of the ground truth interactome and is even compatible with binomially distributed node degrees in the ground truth interactome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The PPI network obtained by aggregating all Y2H studies is not PL-distributed (p=0).
source: A likely explanation for this is that, unlike the PPI network obtained by aggregating all AP-MS studies annotated in IntAct, the PPI network obtained by aggregating all Y2H studies is itself not PL-distributed (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical testing shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The false negative rate did not have a strong effect on the simulation results.
source: For both simulated AP-MS and simulated Y2H testing, the false negative rate did not have a strong effect on the results (see small row-wise variances in the heatmaps shown in Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in the figures.

claim: Active module discovery methods perform equally well on real and random networks in which the node degree is preserved.
source: Furthermore, it was shown that active module discovery methods perform equally well on real and random networks in which the node degree is preserved (Lazareva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a cited finding from the literature.

claim: Y2H and AP-MS account for more than 70% of all reported interactions in the network used in this study.
source: Combined, Y2H and AP-MS account for more than 70% of all reported interactions in the network used here.
evidence: This is a statistic about the data used in the study.

claim: XL-MS does not require bait protein selection.
source: Conversely, cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) does not require bait protein selection.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology of XL-MS.

claim: XL-MS employs chemical cross-linkers on protein complexes within human cellular lysates, with mass spectrometry subsequently identifying peptides in close spatial proximity.
source: XL-MS employs chemical cross-linkers on protein complexes within human cellular lysates, with mass spectrometry (MS) subsequently identifying peptides in close spatial proximity.
evidence: This is a description of the XL-MS methodology.

claim: Techniques that can detect PPIs with an FDR as low as 1% would considerably reduce the technical bias in detecting PPIs.
source: Employing techniques that can detect PPIs with an FDR as low as 1% (Lenz et al., 2021) would considerably reduces the technical bias in detecting PPIs.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on cited methodology.

claim: The HuRI project is currently following a strategy to systematically and objectively study PPIs without prior evidence for the relevance of a protein.
source: An alternative strategy is thus to systematically and objectively study PPIs without prior evidence for the relevance of a protein, a strategy currently followed by the HuRI project (Luck et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a cited example of an alternative approach.
